newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran bracing for Iraqi Kurdish refugee exodus.
newsitem.headline: Iran bracing for Iraqi Kurdish refugee exodus.

text.p: Iran is bracing for an exodus of Iraqi Kurd refugees fleeing heavy inter-Kurdish fighting in northern Iraq, a United Nations official said on Monday.

"Iranian officials are very alarmed and envisage hundreds of thousands of refugees pouring in over the border," said Laurens Jolles, an official of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) office in Tehran.
"But Iranian officials have not confirmed that any refugees were in Iran yet or how many were at the borders," Jolles told Reuters by telephone.
"I was told by our people in Arbil (in northern Iraq) that 2,000 Kurds were already at the border. But I cannot confirm this because we have not had access to border areas," he added.
"No refugees are at the border here," an Iranian official in the border town of Baneh, across from the Iraqi city of Sulaimaniya, told Reuters in Tehran by telephone.

The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) said on Monday its last stronghold Sulaimaniya, 50 km (30 miles) from the Iran border, was in danger of collapse and appealed to Washington to help it against the rival Iraqi-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) which it said was backed by Iraqi forces.
The KDP has denied it was receiving support from Baghdad in the latest round of fighting.
State-run Tehran radio quoted unnamed sources as reporting that 50 Iraqi tanks had backed the KDP drive into Koi Sanjaq.
Jolles said Iranian officials had asked international organisations to be ready for any situation "which might be a parallel to 1991."

In 1991, more than one million Iraqis, most of them Kurds, fled to Iran when Baghdad crushed Kurdish and Shi'ite Moslem uprisings which erupted after Iraq's defeat in the Gulf War. Most of the Kurds have since returned to northern Iraq.
The Tehran daily Kayhan said thousands of refugees were fleeing towards Iran from Sulaimaniya and Koi Sanjaq, which fell to the KDP on Sunday.
"If international organisations do not come to the aid of them (the refugees) there will be a repeat of the 1991 tragedy," the newspaper warned.
UNHCR spokesman in Geneva, Rupert Colville, told the U.S. network CNN that the refugee organisation had very good cooperation with the Iranian authorities.
Tehran last week expressed concern that the clashes might bring about a repeat of the 1991 exodus which burdened a country which already has about 1.5 million Afghan refugees.
Tehran has said that it was spending $2 million a day on refugees and repeatedly complained over insufficient funds for the refugees channelled through the United Nations.
Iran has rejected charges by Iraq and the KDP that it has intervened in northern Iraq by backing the PUK.
Baghdad has said its recent attack on Arbil in northern Iraq, which prompted two waves of punitive U.S. missile strikes on Iraq last week, was aimed at backing the KDP against the PUK and Iran.
